contents.locator: Pedersen Theorems 1–2 pp3–5 and Remark 2 p5; local expansion, not a new source theorem
contents.support: Tychonoff under AC makes the product compact; coordinatewise group operations are continuous by the product universal property, and distinct coordinates separate points, so it is Hausdorff. Apply the local normalized Haar theorem to the entire product. For a finite-coordinate projection pi_F, the pushforward nu(B)=mu(pi_F^{-1}B) is a Borel probability. On a compact space the given outer regularity makes a finite Radon measure inner regular on every Borel set by taking closed complements of approximating open supersets of its complement. For Borel B in the finite subproduct, approximate pi_F^{-1}B by compact K. The compact pi_F(K) lies in B and has nu(pi_F K)>=mu(K), proving inner regularity of nu on Borel sets. Complements give outer regularity too; thus nu is Radon. Lift a finite-product translation using identity elements in all other coordinates, so left invariance of mu proves left invariance of nu. Local uniqueness identifies the finite marginal. Finally, for h continuous on the whole compact product and epsilon>0, take finitely many basic cylinder neighbourhoods covering the product on each of which h oscillates by less than epsilon. Let F contain all their specified coordinates. Points agreeing on F then lie together in one chosen neighbourhood, so their h values differ by less than epsilon. Fill the remaining coordinates by the group identities, obtaining a continuous section s_F and the cylinder h composed with s_F composed with pi_F uniformly within epsilon of h. Equal finite marginals therefore give equal integrals of all continuous h, by the probability error bound, and RMK uniqueness gives equality on all Borel sets. The empty coordinate family gives the one-point group. No equality of product and Borel sigma algebras and no arbitrary product-measure existence theorem is assumed.

Define the integral and measure independently; equivalence is discharged by the later existence and RMK uniqueness results, never assumed in the definition. Real C_c first, then complexification. No global sigma-compactness or second countability.

Translation and inversion are continuous with explicit continuous inverses by the topological-group hypotheses in def-left-haar-integral-and-left-haar-measure. Homeomorphisms carry the closure of the nonzero set onto its closure, giving the exact support formulas. Fix a compact neighbourhood V of a0, supplied by def-locally-compact-space through the defining item. For a in V all left supports lie in VK and all right supports lie in KV^{-1}; these sets are compact by thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces followed by thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps. Their union C is compact: restrict any open cover to each compact set and unite the two finite subcovers. For each x in C the continuous functions H_L(a,x)=f(a^{-1}x)-f(a0^{-1}x) and H_R(a,x)=f(xa)-f(xa0) vanish at (a0,x). For epsilon>0, collect all open rectangles U times W containing (a0,x) on which both absolute values are less than epsilon/2. The W sets cover C; take finitely many rectangles covering C and intersect their U sets with an open neighbourhood of a0 contained in V. This gives one parameter neighbourhood on which both differences are bounded by epsilon/2 on C. Off C all four translated functions vanish, so both uniform norms are at most epsilon/2 < epsilon. If K is empty all functions are zero and the conclusion is immediate. The finite selections are finite choice only. This supplies exactly the uniform/common-support estimates, without using Haar existence, partitions, integration, or a metrizability/sequence assumption.

For f>=0 and nonzero phi>=0 define (f:phi)=inf sum c_j over finite covers f<=sum c_j L_{x_j}phi, c_j>0. Define (0:phi)=0. Fix nonzero f0>=0 and I_phi(f)=(f:phi)/(f0:phi); only use this quotient after the next lemma establishes a positive denominator.

Translate a set where phi>epsilon to cover supp f finitely. Sup norms give (f:phi)>=||f||/||phi||>0. Composition of finite covers proves (f:psi)<=(f:phi)(phi:psi). Include monotonicity, positive homogeneity, subadditivity and exact left invariance. Consequently 1/(f0:f)<=I_phi(f)<=(f:f0) for nonzero f.

Left invariance is EXACT for every approximant, not only asymptotic. Record positivity, homogeneity and I_phi(f0)=1, with coordinate bounds independent of phi. Almost additivity is separately proved in the new supporting lemma.

Assume AC, including the DC used by the inherited cutoff. Take F=1 on supp(f1+f2); set q=f1+f2+delta F and h_i=f_i/q, zero where q=0. Their continuity follows because q>=delta on the support of either numerator. Uniform continuity bounds h_i at the centres of every sufficiently small translate of phi. Split a finite cover of q with coefficients h_i(centre)+eta. The error after normalization is bounded by delta(1+2eta)(F:f0)+2eta(f1+f2:f0). Choose delta,eta before phi. Zero functions are immediate. Knapp Lemma 6.12.

Assume AC. In the product of the coordinate intervals [1/(f0:f),(f:f0)], take closures E_U of all approximants supported in U. All finite intersections contain E_intersection U; cutoffs make each nonempty. Tychonoff and compact-FIP supply a point in their total intersection. Do NOT claim a finite approximant is already additive. Almost additivity passes to the closed limit constraints.

Assume AC. The common point is additive and homogeneous on the positive cone, fixes f0, and is left invariant. Define I(u-v)=I(u)-I(v); u-v=uprime-vprime implies u+vprime=uprime+v, proving independence. Extend complex linearly if desired. This proves existence, not mere boundedness of candidates.

Assume AC inherited from existence and RMK. Represent I. Translate pushforwards are Radon and have the same C_c integrals, so RMK uniqueness gives Borel invariance. Push forward by inversion to obtain a right Haar measure. No inversion invariance of a general left Haar measure is claimed. At the transitive RMK outer-measure step, use the equivalent supremum over 0<=f<=1 with supp(f) compactly contained in U from lem-rmk-functional-outer-content-is-well-defined. This corrects step 1.2 of thm-rmk-functional-outer-content-is-an-outer-measure: the weaker pointwise f<=1_U alone does not imply supp(f) is contained in U. For U=union U_n, a compact support contained in U has a finite subcover with distinct indices; the finite LCH partition splits f into admissible functions for these U_n, giving Lambda(f)<=sum rho(U_n). Taking this equivalent supremum and choosing open approximations with errors epsilon*2^(-n-1) proves outer subadditivity under the stated AC. The remaining RMK representation and uniqueness clauses apply unchanged.

A nonzero Haar integral is strictly positive on every nonzero nonnegative test function: compare f0 to finite translates of that function. For a measure, a zero nonempty open set would make every compact set null by finite translates; open inner and Borel outer regularity would force the entire measure to be zero. Compact finiteness is part of the definition.

Let K_X,K_Y be the compact projections of supp F; if either is empty F=0. Choose compactly supported cutoffs 0<=c_X,c_Y<=1 equal to one on these projections. For fixed y_0, continuity on the compact K_X gives a neighbourhood V of y_0 with sup_x |F(x,y)-F(x,y_0)|<epsilon for y in V: take finitely many continuity rectangles covering K_X and intersect their parameter neighbourhoods; outside K_X both functions vanish. Cover L_Y=supp c_Y by finitely many such V_j with chosen centres y_j. Use the published finite partition lemma on L_Y, obtaining nonnegative psi_j supported in V_j with sum psi_j=1 on L_Y. Define G(x,y)=c_Y(y) sum_j psi_j(y)F(x,y_j). Then G is a finite tensor sum with support in K_X times L_Y, and |F-G|<=epsilon c_X(x)c_Y(y) everywhere: F=c_Y F, the convex-combination estimate holds on L_Y, and outside K_X or L_Y both sides vanish. Partial integrals exist since each section is in C_c. Their continuity follows directly from the same uniform section estimate and positivity, e.g. |I(F_y)-I(F_y0)|<=epsilon I(c_X); their supports lie in K_Y or K_X. Thus no undeclared uniform-limit theorem is needed. The two iterated integrals of G agree by linearity on its finite tensor sum. AC covers precisely the inherited cutoff and partition selections; all new covers are finite. No measure-product theorem, Stone–Weierstrass or sigma-compactness is used.

Apply I to every finite translate cover of f by g and take the coefficient-sum infimum. For the sharp inequality, the kernel F(x,y)=f(x)u(x^{-1}y) is continuous with compact support contained in supp f times (supp f)(supp u). First integrate y by left invariance to obtain I(f)J(u). Interchange the compact kernel, and then substitute x=yz using left invariance of I. Symmetry gives u(z^{-1})=u(z), so the result is J_y I_z f(yz)u(z). contents.support: Put A_R=(kG)^R and B_R=kC_G(R). This proof works over any field k, hence under the inherited splitting p-modular hypotheses, without a nilpotent-kernel assumption. First prove the following general fact inside this item, not by a later commutative-algebra supplier. If phi:A onto B is a unital homomorphism of finite-dimensional k-algebras, every idempotent y of B lifts to an idempotent of A. The cases y=0,1 use 0,1. Otherwise choose x above y. Linear dependence of 1,x,...,x^dim(A) gives a nonzero polynomial m with m(x)=0. Since m(y)=m(0)(1-y)+m(1)y=0 and both y and 1-y are nonzero, multiplication by these two idempotents gives m(0)=m(1)=0. Write m(T)=g(T)(T-1)^s, where s>=1 is maximal; then g(1) is nonzero and g(0)=0. Polynomial Bezout gives u*g+v*(T-1)^s=1. For q=u*g, q(q-1)=-u*v*m, q(0)=0, q(1)=1. Consequently q(x) is an idempotent lifting q(y)=y. Evaluation is legitimate in a noncommutative algebra because powers of one element commute and k is central. No division by 2 occurs.  For an idempotent e of A, the restriction eAe onto phi(e)Bphi(e) is surjective: phi(eae)=phi(e)phi(a)phi(e). Its identity is e and its kernel is e(ker phi)e. Apply the same polynomial proof in this finite-dimensional corner, interpreting scalar constants as multiples of e. If e is primitive and its nonzero image were not primitive, a nontrivial idempotent in the image corner would lift to u in eAe, with u neither 0 nor e. But e=u+(e-u) is a nontrivial orthogonal decomposition, contradiction. Thus primitive idempotents have zero or primitive images under every such surjection. Conversely, lifting and then finitely decomposing any primitive target idempotent gives a primitive lift: exactly one summand survives.  Orthogonality and sums are preserved by phi; deleting zero summands thus gives a primitive decomposition of the image. The coefficient Brauer map A_R onto B_R is surjective since it fixes B_R, and is multiplicative by the preceding theorem. Apply the general fact first to a decomposition of 1 in A_R, then to a primitive decomposition of i in A_Q. Primitivity of a summand j<=i in iA_Qi equals primitivity in A_Q, since jA_Qj is the same corner in either algebra. Empty surviving families represent zero. This proves both retained clauses without asserting that b_Q(i) itself is primitive when i was only primitive in A_P.

alternatives.argument: Work over the given splitting residue field k, finite G, characteristic p. The left double action is (x,y).a=xay^{-1}. Central b makes kGb a summand. Bimodule endomorphisms identify with bZ(kG); primitive central b makes this commutative finite-dimensional algebra local, hence kGb indecomposable. Prove the local-ring assertion by the Fitting decomposition, as in Krull-Schmidt, not by assuming simplicity.
The map k[(G times G)/Delta G] to kG sending (x,y)Delta G to xy^{-1} is well-defined, equivariant, and bijective on bases. Thus kG=Ind_DeltaG^{G times G} k.

Work with finite groups and finite-dimensional left modules over k. Write X divides Y to mean X is isomorphic to a direct summand of Y. Restriction and induction preserve this relation, by applying the functors to split inclusion and projection maps. A summand of a relatively A-projective module is again relatively A-projective. Higman's counit criterion ensures that relative projectivity can always be witnessed using the finite module Res_A X. For A,B subgroups of H and a kB-module V, choose a finite set of double-coset representatives x in A\H/B. Set L_x=A intersect xBx^{-1}. Regard V as an L_x-module by t.v=(x^{-1}tx)v; equivalently this is the conjugate of its restriction to B intersect x^{-1}Ax. There is an isomorphism $\operatorname{Res}_A^H\operatorname{Ind}_B^H V\cong\bigoplus_{x\in A\backslash H/B}\operatorname{Ind}_{L_x}^A({}^x\operatorname{Res}_{B\cap x^{-1}Ax}^B V).$ On the x-term its map is a tensor v to ax tensor v. It is well-defined since atx tensor v=ax tensor (x^{-1}tx)v for t in L_x. The group-algebra basis partitions into disjoint double cosets AxB, giving a direct sum of (kA,kB)-bimodules. Within AxB, left coset representatives for A/L_x give a right kB-basis ax: if a_1xB=a_2xB then a_2^{-1}a_1 belongs to L_x. Thus both sides of this component map are the same direct sum of copies of V and the map is bijective. This establishes the module isomorphism in arbitrary characteristic, not merely an equality of ordinary characters. Induction transitivity is the explicit isomorphism a tensor (b tensor v) maps to ab tensor v, with inverse a tensor v maps to a tensor (1 tensor v). All tensor relations are respected. Hence relative projectivity is transitive up a subgroup chain. For completeness the vertex-containment consequence does not require an unsupported restriction inference. Suppose indecomposable M has vertex Q and is also relatively B-projective. The two counit retractions and their images under induction/restriction show $M\mid\operatorname{Ind}_Q^H\operatorname{Res}_Q^H\operatorname{Ind}_B^H\operatorname{Res}_B^H M.$ Mackey in the middle and transitivity express the right side as a finite sum of modules induced to H from Q intersect xBx^{-1}. Krull–Schmidt makes M a summand of one such term. Since this subgroup is a p-subgroup of Q, minimality of Q forces Q=Q intersect xBx^{-1}. Thus Q is contained in xBx^{-1}, as required. The same finite-sum extraction may be justified by the local endomorphism-ring clause in the published Krull–Schmidt proof: write identity as the sum of component inclusion/projection composites; some composite is a unit, giving a split factorization through one term.

The block summand is relatively Delta G-projective. The containment lemma puts some vertex inside Delta G; any such p-subgroup is Delta D. Do not identify a mere relatively projective subgroup with a minimal vertex.
Define defect groups from diagonal vertices and d by |D|=p^d. This is a definition for kGb; any lattice identification is outside this definition unless separately proved.

Vertex conjugacy in G times G gives conjugacy of diagonal subgroups; projection to the first factor gives G-conjugacy of their component subgroups. Conversely diagonal conjugation transports the vertex.

Restriction from G times G to Delta G preserves relative Delta H-projectivity: Mackey intersections are diagonals of subgroups of conjugates of H. Higman evaluated at b gives the trace equality. Conversely left multiplication by a supplies a Delta H endomorphism with trace identity. Combine this with relative Delta G-projectivity and induction transitivity. Minimality recovers defects. Webb Lemma 12.4.4/Theorem 12.4.5, specialized to k.
Write b=Tr_D^G(a). On M with bM=M, multiplication by a is D-linear and has G-trace identity, so M is relatively D-projective. Apply vertex containment. Finite-dimensional indecomposable M only.

The principal idempotent is the unique block acting as 1 on the trivial module. For that module the relative trace is multiplication by [G:H], so its vertices are Sylow p-subgroups. Containment forces the principal block to have Sylow defect.

Defect one makes every block module projective by vertex containment and Higman, hence B is semisimple and, because b is primitive central, one split matrix factor. For the reverse simple-projective implication, restrict the symmetric coefficient form to B, use projective equals injective and the regular-projective decomposition, then symmetric Cartan duality makes the projective-simple isotypic summand a central direct factor; block indecomposability removes its complement. For the matrix-to-defect implication use the enveloping factor B tensor B-op, identified with b tensor b-star by the group involution.

For a p-subgroup P define Br_P on (kG)^P by retaining coefficients at C_G(P). Codomain is the full centralizer group algebra. Multiplicativity is an obligation proved next; it is false to define the same projection as a homomorphism on all of kG.

Expand a product at z in C_G(P). P acts diagonally on pairs (x,y) with xy=z; coefficients are constant on orbits. Every non-singleton orbit has size divisible by p, while singleton pairs have x,y in C_G(P). This proves the coefficient identity. The map is unital and surjective because it fixes kC_G(P).
Conjugation carries C_G(P) to C_G(gPg^{-1}) and permutes the corresponding coefficient basis. Write the equality with left conjugation consistently.

A primitive decomposition of 1 in A_P provides at least one i with b_P(i)e nonzero, since the corresponding sum is e. Such i has b_P(i)e=b_P(i). For Q<=P, b_P(i) nonzero implies b_Q(i) nonzero by C_G(P) subset C_G(Q); this does not assert a relative map on all of B_Q when Q is not normal.  The needed primitive-corner nilpotence assertion also has a direct proof over arbitrary k. Let C=iA_Pi with i primitive, and c in C. For sufficiently large n the kernels and images of left multiplication L_c^n stabilize. Their intersection is zero: c^n x in the kernel implies c^(2n)x=0, so x is in ker L_c^n and c^n x=0. Rank-nullity gives C=ker L_c^n direct-sum im L_c^n. Both are right C-submodules, so the projection onto either is left multiplication by its value at i, an idempotent. Primitivity forces one summand zero. Hence c is nilpotent or L_c is bijective. In the latter case cx=i for some x; injectivity applied to c(xc-i)=0 gives xc=i, so c is a unit. Every element of any proper two-sided ideal of C is therefore nilpotent. We need no radical theorem and make no claim that an arbitrary Brauer kernel is nilpotent.  For Q<=P and N=N_P(Q), coefficient counting gives the exact identity      b_Q(Tr_Q^P(a)) = Tr_Q^N(b_Q(a))  (a in A_Q).  Indeed Q acts on the cosets P/Q indexing the trace. Those remaining summands give the displayed identity, using conjugation equivariance of b_Q. In particular the two image spaces are equal because b_Q is onto B_Q. More generally, if (Q,f) preceq (P,e), (S,d) preceq (P,e), and (S,d') preceq (Q,f), then d=d'. Choose associated i of A_P and decompose i into primitive j's in A_Q. This compatibility argument uses no transitivity or arbitrary-subgroup existence.  ### Normal inclusions  If Q is normal in P, the earlier normal-subpair theorem supplies the unique P-stable block f with Br_(P/Q)(f)e=e. The restriction b_Q:A_P onto (B_Q)^P is surjective: every element of (B_Q)^P already lies in A_P and is fixed by b_Q. Its uniqueness proves the converse normal characterization. It is essential here to use primitivity in the **fixed target algebra**; b_Q(i) need not be primitive in B_Q.  ### Arbitrary subgroup existence: the missing normalizer/trace argument  Induct on [P:Q]. The equality and normal cases are settled. For a proper nonnormal Q let N=N_P(Q). One has Q<N<P: Q acting on P/Q has [N:Q] fixed cosets, and fixed-point congruence modulo p gives p dividing [N:Q]. Fix any primitive i associated to (P,e), and put z=b_Q(i)(1-f). This is an N-fixed idempotent of B_Q. For Q<R<=N, compatibility at R gives b_R(i)e_R=b_R(i), hence Br_(R/Q)(z)=0. Thus O_p(K) is contained in every Sylow p-subgroup. Apply this with K=G and intersect the two Sylow subgroups in the preceding lemma to obtain O_p(G) contained in D.
